newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong handover won't silence noonday gun.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong handover won't silence noonday gun.

text.p: Reports the handover of Hong Kong to China will silence the famous Jardine Noonday Gun, immortalised by writer Noel Coward in his song "Mad Dogs and Englishmen", are a myth.
Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd, the venerable colonial trading firm with a buccaneering history tied up with the founding of Hong Kong, has no such intention.
"There are no plans to change the Noonday Gun," Jardine managing director Alasdair Morrison said on Monday.

Noel Coward visited Hong Kong in 1929 and in the same year penned "Mad Dogs and Englishmen", which contains the lines -"In Hong Kong they strike a gong and fire off a noonday gun to reprimand each inmate Who's in late."
The legend often trotted out in Hong Kong about the gun is probably also a myth, historians say.
The story goes that an overenthusiastic Jardines employee fired off a 21-gun salute, reserved for royalty only, to greet the arrival of the taipan, as the Jardines' chief was known.
As punishment, an enraged British Admiral ordered the company to fire a cannon each day at noon.
In reality, historians believe the company probably agreed to relieve the military of the chore of marking midday.

Jardine Matheson was the first of the powerful big trading companies to move its headquarters from Canton (Guangzhou) to the new colony of Hong Kong, annexed in 1841 as a result of the first Sino-British Opium war.
The present-day gun now sits on a spit of land close to that original plot in what was then called East Point but is now known as Causeway Bay.

The original cannon disappeared during the Japanese occupation of Hong Kong in World War Two but the Royal Navy stepped in and replaced it with a suitable six-pounder. Jardines resumed the tradition in August 1947.
In 1961, following complaints about the noise, the Hong Kong Marine police presented the company with a quieter Hotchkiss Mark 1 three-pound quick firing gun.
This was the gun that Coward, by then Sir Noel, was invited to fire when he visited Hong Kong on holiday in 1968.
Local historian Arthur Hacker says he was late -- and so was the noonday gun that day. It boomed out at three minutes past the hour.
